name: Kingdom of Serbia
info: A Balkan monarchy proclaimed in 1882 that doubled its lands in the Balkan Wars, was overrun in World War I and merged in 1918 into the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes.

facts.successor: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes (later the Kingdom of Yugoslavia)

t: Serbia was raised from a principality to a kingdom in 1882 under Milan I of the House of Obrenović.
The May Coup of 1903 killed King Alexander I and Queen Draga, brought Peter I of the Karađorđević dynasty to the throne and turned Serbia from Austria-Hungary towards Russia and France.
In the Balkan Wars of 1912–1913 Serbia's population rose from 2.9 million to 4.5 million and its territory by 81%, with Kosovo, Sandžak and Vardar Macedonia annexed.
dyk: By the beginning of the 1880s Serbia and Montenegro were the only European nations without railroads; one conservative deputy warned that building them would make Serbia suffer the fate of the Indians after the discovery of America.
ev: Milan I is proclaimed king and the Principality of Serbia becomes a kingdom
Serbia is defeated by Bulgaria in the Serbo-Bulgarian War after the Battle of Slivnitsa
Milan I abdicates and is succeeded by his son Alexander I
In the May Coup officers kill King Alexander I and Queen Draga; Peter Karađorđević becomes Peter I
Austria-Hungary imposes the Tariff War, the Pig war, on Serbia
Serbia fights the First and Second Balkan Wars and annexes Kosovo, Sandžak and Vardar Macedonia
Austro-Hungarian, German and Bulgarian troops occupy Serbia; the army retreats through Albania to Corfu
On 1 December Serbia unites with the State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs to form the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes

sections.foundation:
The kingdom grew out of the Principality of Serbia, created by the Serbian revolution of 1804–1817 under Karađorđe and then Miloš Obrenović, and ruled from 1817 by the Obrenović dynasty. The principality, under Ottoman suzerainty, gained de facto independence when the last Ottoman garrisons left in 1867, and the Congress of Berlin in 1878 recognised its formal independence and added the districts of Nišava, Pirot, Toplica and Vranje. In the newly gained areas an estimated 49,000–130,000 Albanians were expelled, settling mainly in Kosovo, events that marked the beginning of the Serbian-Albanian conflict; from 1830 to 1876 up to 150,000 Albanians had already emigrated or been expelled from the principality.

In 1882 the ruler of the principality, Milan I, was proclaimed king. The new kingdom at first kept a foreign policy friendly to Austria-Hungary, in whose political and economic sphere it lay until 1903. Its elite was divided between liberals, who looked to the West, and conservatives, who looked back to an idealised medieval Serbian empire.
sections.socioeconomy:
Serbia was a predominantly agrarian society, most of its people living in extended families called zadruga, communities of property, work and authority in which fathers and grandfathers held absolute power. After independence the estates of the Muslim aristocracy were broken up, so that, unusually for Eastern Europe, the peasantry owned its land, though through the zadruga. The population rose by 71.3% between 1880 and 1914, one of the highest birthrates in Europe, and poverty was extreme: between 1910 and 1914 two thirds of farmers could not reach an existential minimum, and by January–February about 46% of rural Serbs suffered food insecurity.

The national debt rose from 16.5 million francs in 1880 to 903.8 million in 1914, and Belgrade had only six millionaires besides the royal family in 1900. The Congress of Berlin obliged Serbia to build the railway from Belgrade to Vranje; Serbian Railways were formed in 1881 and regular traffic between Belgrade and Niš began in 1884. The Morava Valley carried the route linking Central Europe with Greece and Constantinople.
sections.military:
The Serbo-Bulgarian War of 14–28 November 1885 ended in defeat. The Bulgarians won the decisive Battle of Slivnitsa and advanced to take Pirot, and withdrew only when Austria-Hungary declared it would join on Serbia's side; the peace of Bucharest of 19 February 1886 left the border unchanged. In 1912 Serbia allied with Bulgaria, Greece and Montenegro. In the First Balkan War it took Pristina and Novi Pazar, defeated the Ottoman army at the Battle of Kumanovo and conquered Skopje and the Kosovo vilayet. Lazër Mjeda, Archbishop of Skopje, estimated that 25,000 Albanians were killed by Serbian forces during and after the conflict.

In the Second Balkan War of 1913 Serbia, Greece, Romania, the Ottoman Empire and Montenegro fought Bulgaria over Macedonia. After Austria-Hungary declared war on 28 July 1914, a combined Austro-Hungarian, German and Bulgarian invasion occupied Serbia in 1915. The 135,000 soldiers of the Serbian Army retreated through Albania to Corfu and in 1916 joined the Salonika front. Serbia lost 28% of its pre-war population in the war.
sections.governance:
Two dynasties ruled the kingdom. Milan I reigned from 6 March 1882 until his abdication on 6 March 1889, after the lost war and the total electoral victory of the People's Radical Party, which under Sava Grujić and Nikola Pašić had come to power in 1888 with a new constitution based on the liberal Constitution of Belgium. His son Alexander I, who succeeded him, assumed the throne in 1893 and dismissed the constitution in 1894. On the night of 28–29 May 1903 officers killed Alexander I and Queen Draga in the Royal Palace in Belgrade, ending the House of Obrenović.

The Skupština then invited Peter Karađorđević, who reigned as Peter I from 15 June 1903 to 1 December 1918. A constitutional monarchy was created, with the military Black Hand society operating behind the scenes; the People's Radical Party governed after the 1906 elections. In 1890 the country was divided into 15 districts (okruzi) and counties (srezovi), Belgrade and Niš having special status; in August 1913 eleven new districts were formed in the conquered lands, and Jews in present-day North Macedonia gained citizen rights.
sections.impact:
After 1903 the new dynasty relied on the Russian Empire and closer cooperation with Bulgaria, signing a friendship treaty in 1904 and a customs union in 1905; Austria-Hungary answered with the Pig war. Its annexation of Bosnia and Herzegovina in October 1908, where Serbia had hoped to expand, set off the Bosnian Crisis of 1908–1909, which permanently damaged relations between Austria-Hungary and Russia and Serbia and was among the causes of World War I. The Treaty of London of May 1913 recognised Kosovo and north-western Macedonia as Serbian, and the Treaty of Bucharest of 1913 gave it Vardar Macedonia, though the new Principality of Albania kept it from the Adriatic.

On 28 June 1914 Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated in Sarajevo, an act behind which stood the secret Serbian officers' organisation Black Hand, which aimed to break the South Slav provinces away from Austria-Hungary. The assassination set off the chain of events that drew Russia and the major European powers into war. In culture, Serbian artists including Ivan Meštrović showed in the Serbian pavilion at the International Exhibition of Art of 1911.
sections.decline:
The kingdom ended not in defeat but in union. After the collapse of Austria-Hungary at the end of World War I, Serbia, which had lost 28% of its pre-war population, went through radical changes within days of its liberation. In 1916 Montenegro had been conquered by Austria-Hungary. Serbia united with Vojvodina, and on 28 November 1918 it absorbed the Kingdom of Montenegro at the Podgorica Assembly.

On 1 December 1918 Serbia united with the newly created State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs to form the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, later known as the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. Peter I's reign over Serbia ended that day, the day the new kingdom was proclaimed. The new country continued under the Serbian monarchy of the Karađorđević dynasty, and in August 1921 Prince Alexandar I became king. The territories Serbia had annexed in 1912–1913, among them Kosovo and Vardar Macedonia, passed with it into the new state; Vardar Macedonia is today the independent Republic of North Macedonia.

summary: The Kingdom of Serbia, proclaimed under Milan I in 1882, was a poor agrarian monarchy of zadruga households, ruled first by the Obrenović and from the May Coup of 1903 by the Karađorđević dynasty. It nearly doubled in the Balkan Wars, was overrun in 1915 and in 1918 formed the core of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes.
references: Calic, Marie-Janine, A History of Yugoslavia (Purdue University, 2019)
Rama, Shinasi, Nation Failure, Ethnic Elites, and Balance of Power: The International Administration of Kosova (Springer, 2019)

pointDescs.1882: Milan I is proclaimed king of Serbia.
pointDescs.1885: Serbia loses the Serbo-Bulgarian War after the Battle of Slivnitsa.
pointDescs.1889: Milan I abdicates in favour of his son Alexander I.
pointDescs.1903: The May Coup ends the Obrenović line; Peter I begins a constitutional reign and Serbia turns towards Russia.
pointDescs.1908: Austria-Hungary annexes Bosnia and Herzegovina, opening the Bosnian Crisis.
pointDescs.1912: In the First Balkan War Serbia wins at Kumanovo and conquers Skopje and the Kosovo vilayet.
pointDescs.1913: The Treaties of London and Bucharest confirm Serbia's gains; its territory grows by 81%.
pointDescs.1914: After the assassination in Sarajevo, Austria-Hungary declares war on Serbia on 28 July.
pointDescs.1915: Austro-Hungarian, German and Bulgarian troops occupy Serbia; the army retreats to Corfu.
pointDescs.1916: The Serbian Army joins the new Salonika front.
pointDescs.1918: Serbia absorbs Montenegro and on 1 December forms the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes.

notes: Capital Belgrade is implied by the article (Royal Palace in Belgrade, Belgrade's special status) rather than stated as 'capital'. Alexander I's 1893 accession is how the article puts it although it also says he ruled from 1889; I kept both, as the article does. The Gavrilović article in Serbian omitted from references (a journal paper).
